case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in determining intellectual disability under Atkins, a court may (or must) evaluate multiple IQ scores cumulatively/holistically—rather than score-by-score—and what role, if any, non-IQ evidence plays in that cumulative assessment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as implemented through Atkins v. Virginia and subsequent intellectual-disability death-penalty cases); related federal analogue referenced: 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) (Federal Death Penalty Act bar on executing intellectually disabled defendants).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama argues that its framework properly requires a defendant to show a likelihood (not mere possibility) that the true IQ is 70 or below when multiple IQ scores exist, and that courts may consider the cumulative pattern of scores to determine whether the intellectual-functioning prong is satisfied; on Alabama’s view, respondent’s repeated scores in the 70s (e.g., 72–78 range) do not make it likely his true IQ is ≤70, so the courts below erred by letting the claim proceed based on a theoretical possibility that measurement error could place him at or below 70 and by effectively treating IQ as satisfied once any score could be SEM-adjusted downward.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that Atkins and this Court’s follow-on decisions require courts to avoid rigid IQ cutoffs and instead evaluate IQ scores consistent with clinical standards, including the standard error of measurement, and then consider the full body of relevant evidence (including other evidence of intellectual functioning and adaptive functioning) rather than using multiple above-70 scores as a categorical bar; he contends the lower courts correctly recognized that, given test imprecision and the record, his intellectual-disability claim cannot be rejected simply because several scores are above 70.
key_precedents: Moore v. Texas, 139 S. Ct. 666 (2019) (per curiam)
Powell v. Texas, 392 U.S. 514 (1968) (plurality) (referenced for "fruitful experimentation")
Clark v. Sweeney (summary reversal referenced in oral argument excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor forcefully argue that Alabama’s “likelihood” screen could operate as an indirect bright-line cutoff, effectively barring adaptive-deficits and other clinically relevant evidence whenever multiple scores cluster just above 70. I agree that Hall and Moore prohibit any application that makes low-70s scores function as a stop-sign despite SEM, but those precedents do not require respondent’s broader rule that any SEM-overlapping score automatically guarantees prong-two litigation regardless of the full IQ record; Atkins preserves meaningful state discretion so long as procedures do not create an unacceptable risk of executing the intellectually disabled. A narrow reversal and remand—requiring a genuine preponderance/likelihood application while expressly forbidding treating SEM-overlapping scores as dispositively above 70—addresses the operational defect Kagan identifies without constitutionalizing a particular sequencing protocol. Because the constitutional vice is categorical foreclosure, not holistic evidentiary weighing, I do not find the respondent bloc’s reading sufficiently grounded in our holdings to justify affirmance on broader terms.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the strongest point that Alabama’s “likelihood” screen could, in operation, become a de facto cutoff that prevents consideration of adaptive deficits in close-threshold cases, which Hall and Moore disallow. But as Chief Justice Roberts argues, Hall’s holding is directed at rigid numerical bars and demands only a fair opportunity to present clinically relevant evidence when SEM places the defendant near 70; it does not constitutionalize respondent’s rule that any SEM overlap automatically entitles the defendant to proceed to prong two regardless of the full IQ record. Under Atkins’s explicit reservation of implementation to the States—and because neither the Eighth Amendment’s text nor its original public meaning speaks to SEM margins or prong sequencing—the proper course is a narrow reversal/remand to ensure the standard is not applied categorically, not the broader respondent approach that would nationalize clinical guidance as constitutional command. I therefore remain with Petitioner while emphasizing that any application treating multiple low-70s scores as dispositive above 70 would violate Hall/Moore’s anti–de facto-cutoff principle.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that Alabama’s prong-one “likelihood” screen can operate in practice as a de facto cutoff that blocks the “additional evidence” Hall contemplates—is a real concern, and any rigid treatment of SEM-overlapping scores as dispositively above 70 would be inconsistent with Hall and Moore. But those precedents prohibit categorical rules and nonclinical gatekeeping; they do not constitutionalize a sequencing mandate or a one-way entitlement to reach adaptive-functioning evidence whenever any score, adjusted for SEM, could touch 70, regardless of the full IQ record. Chief Justice Roberts’s approach best addresses the constitutional vice by reversing and remanding with clear direction that SEM and score imprecision must be meaningfully considered and cannot be used as a numerical stop-sign, while still respecting Atkins’s allocation of implementation discretion to the States and allowing holistic weighing under a true preponderance/likelihood standard. Under a textualist, institutionally cautious method, expanding Hall/Moore into a national rule about prong sequencing would overread those cases and unduly displace state procedural judgments without a clearer constitutional command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow remand is the strongest case for Petitioner because it tries to preserve Atkins’s state leeway while policing only truly categorical rules, and I take seriously Justice Alito’s point that Hall/Moore do not constitutionalize a one-score entitlement or a single psychometric protocol. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett explain, the constitutional defect we must police is operational: if Alabama’s “likelihood/preponderance” screen allows multiple low-70s scores to function as a gatekeeping stop-sign, it effectively forecloses the “additional evidence” Hall requires once SEM places the defendant plausibly at 70, recreating Moore’s unacceptable risk through nonclinical narrowing. A remand that merely tells Alabama to apply a ‘true’ preponderance standard without clarifying that SEM-overlap must open a meaningful path to clinically informed interpretation and adaptive-deficits evidence risks blessing the same de facto cutoff under a different label. Because my approach centers on real-world reliability and fair access to the protected Atkins class, I remain with Respondent unless the disposition squarely prevents that truncation rather than inviting it.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s narrow remand is the strongest opposing argument because it purports to enforce Hall/Moore while preserving Atkins’s state discretion, and I agree (as Justice Gorsuch stresses) that those cases do not constitutionalize any single multi-score methodology. But Justice Barrett is right that the defect we are policing is operational: a “likelihood/preponderance” prong-one screen can still function as a de facto cutoff if it treats a cluster of low-70s scores as dispositive before the defendant can present the SEM/validity context and other clinically relevant evidence Hall requires once the record plausibly implicates the zone around 70. On my pragmatic textualist view, Hall’s prohibition is not merely against explicit bright lines but against using IQ evidence “in a way that” forecloses the rest of the Atkins inquiry in close cases, and a remand that invites that truncation under a different label risks underenforcing our precedent. I therefore remain with Respondent because the safer, precedent-coherent rule is to require a meaningful opportunity to present the additional evidence in SEM-overlap cases, without dictating the State’s ultimate weighing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press the most serious objection: that Alabama’s “likelihood” screen could, in operation, become the very sort of de facto cutoff Hall and Moore forbid by stopping the inquiry whenever low-70s scores predominate. But under a principled reading of those precedents (and Atkins’s explicit reservation of implementation space to the States), the constitutional line is not crossed by requiring the defendant to prove prong one by a true preponderance on the whole IQ record; it is crossed only if the State treats above-70 scores as dispositive in a way that forecloses clinically relevant context and additional evidence. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow reversal/remand—clarifying that SEM-overlapping scores cannot be used as a categorical stop-sign while preserving holistic, record-wide weighing—best enforces Hall/Moore without constitutionalizing prong sequencing or turning measurement error into a one-way entitlement. Justice Sotomayor’s “fair opportunity” point is correct as far as it goes, but it does not compel the respondent’s broader rule that any SEM overlap automatically unlocks prong two regardless of the rest of the record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow remand is the strongest petitioner argument because it seeks to respect Atkins’s state latitude and avoid constitutionalizing a rigid scoring protocol, and I agree with him (and Justices Alito and Gorsuch) that Hall/Moore do not compel a one-score entitlement rule. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress, the constitutional problem is operational: a “likelihood/preponderance” screen that treats a cluster of low-70s scores as a practical stop-sign can still foreclose the clinically relevant validity/SEM context and adaptive-deficits evidence Hall requires once the record plausibly reaches 70. A remand that potentially blesses that truncation risks underenforcing Hall’s anti–de facto cutoff principle and Moore’s “unacceptable risk” warning, even while purporting to be narrow and legitimacy-preserving. Under my institutionalist stare decisis approach, the safer course is to enforce the constitutional floor against numeric gatekeeping in close-threshold cases without dictating a single methodology, which keeps me with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s narrow remand proposal is the strongest petitioner-side position because it aims to respect Atkins’s state-implementation discretion while avoiding any bright-line cutoff, and I agree Hall/Moore do not constitutionalize a single psychometric algorithm. But Justice Kagan is right that Hall prohibits using IQ evidence “in a way that” forecloses the additional clinically relevant evidence once SEM places the defendant in the zone of imprecision; a “likelihood/preponderance” gate keyed to aggregating multiple low-70s scores risks functioning as the same stop-sign in operation, not merely in form. Justice Alito’s federalism point is substantial, yet under stare decisis we must enforce Hall’s anti–de facto-cutoff principle: States cannot achieve indirectly—through threshold screening that truncates validity and adaptive-functioning inquiry—what Hall forbids directly. Because the petitioner-side remand does not adequately police that operational risk, I would affirm relief for Respondent (or at minimum require a remand that expressly precludes any prong-one method that categorically blocks prong-two evidence when SEM-adjusted scores plausibly reach 70).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow remand has real force as an institutional, federalism-respecting effort to avoid constitutionalizing a single psychometric protocol, and I take Justice Alito’s point that Hall/Moore do not announce a one-score entitlement rule. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, the constitutional defect we have policed is operational: a prong-one “likelihood/preponderance” screen that treats a cluster of low-70s scores as dispositive can still function as the de facto numerical gatekeeping Hall condemned by foreclosing the “additional, clinically relevant evidence” once SEM makes 70 plausibly in play. Under my procedural-fairness and practical-consequences lens, a remand that invites States to truncate validity and adaptive-functioning evidence in close cases recreates the same unacceptable risk of wrongful execution Moore warned against. Nothing in Atkins’s state-discretion premise authorizes procedures that, in practice, convert measurement imprecision into a one-way stop-sign at the threshold.

John Roberts.reasoning: Hall v. Florida and Moore require that when an IQ score falls within the test’s standard error of measurement, the defendant must be permitted to present additional evidence and the State may not impose a rigid cutoff that makes an above-70 score categorically dispositive. But those cases do not constitutionalize any particular holistic “multiple-score” methodology or reduce the defendant’s burden to a mere showing that his true IQ “could” be 70 or below; Alabama may, consistent with federalism and our precedent, require proof by a preponderance that the defendant’s true IQ is likely at or below 70 before proceeding further. Given the lower courts’ apparent use of a “possibility” standard and the confusion about what arguments were properly preserved, the narrowest course is to reverse and remand for application of the correct likelihood/preponderance standard without foreclosing consideration of non-IQ evidence where IQ data are inconclusive. This approach respects Atkins’s constitutional floor while avoiding an unnecessary, nationwide rule about cumulative scoring methods.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Atkins left the States with substantial discretion to define and implement procedures for determining intellectual disability, and neither Hall v. Florida nor Moore v. Texas purports to constitutionalize a one-low-score rule that treats the intellectual-functioning prong as satisfied whenever any single score can be adjusted downward by the SEM. Hall requires that each score be interpreted with its standard error of measurement and forbids rigid cutoffs that preclude consideration of the claim, but it does not bar a court from evaluating multiple scores cumulatively to decide whether it is likely the defendant’s true IQ is at or below 70. Moore similarly condemns non-clinical distortions and demands attention to prevailing medical standards, yet it does not eliminate the State’s ability to weigh the pattern of reliable scores and related evidence in deciding whether the intellectual-functioning threshold has been met; Alabama’s approach, as described, is consistent with that flexibility and avoids turning SEM into an automatic ticket to further litigation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia forbids executing persons with intellectual disability, and our Eighth Amendment cases require States to implement that protection in a manner consistent with prevailing clinical standards rather than rigid, outcome-driven rules. Hall v. Florida specifically rejected treating an IQ score as a fixed cutoff and held that when a score falls within the test’s standard error of measurement, the defendant must have a fair opportunity to present additional evidence, including adaptive-functioning evidence, before the claim can be rejected. Moore v. Texas reinforces that courts must not use nonclinical, narrowing constructions that create an undue risk of executing an intellectually disabled person; Alabama’s "likelihood" screen, if used to treat multiple above-70 scores as a practical bar notwithstanding SEM, risks exactly that and improperly truncates the inquiry. A holistic assessment may consider multiple scores and other evidence, but it cannot be deployed to foreclose consideration of adaptive deficits where SEM places the defendant plausibly at or below the relevant threshold, because that would elevate administrability over the Constitution’s demand for reliability in capital sentencing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas make clear that Atkins forbids treating an IQ score above 70 as dispositive when, accounting for the test’s standard error of measurement, the defendant’s scores fall in a range that could include 70—because that would recreate the kind of rigid cutoff Hall rejected. Alabama may consider multiple scores in a sensible, clinically informed way, but its “likelihood” gloss, as applied by the courts below, risks converting measurement imprecision into a categorical bar and short-circuiting the broader inquiry these cases require. Under Hall’s emphasis on clinical standards and Moore’s insistence on considering the medical community’s framework, courts must be able to look beyond any single score (or a pattern of scores) to other evidence bearing on intellectual and adaptive functioning once the IQ evidence places the defendant in the relevant imprecision range. That approach is also more workable and coherent, avoiding a state-by-state ratchet that lets aggregation become a one-way tool to deny consideration of the full Atkins claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Atkins forbids executing the intellectually disabled but deliberately left States “the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce the constitutional restriction,” and nothing in the Eighth Amendment’s text or Atkins’ original allocation of authority converts IQ testing into a one-score, one-directional presumption. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas reject rigid cutoffs and “wholly nonclinical” devices for narrowing a single test’s range, but they do not require a court to treat any SEM-adjusted possibility from one score as dispositive when the record contains multiple, more probative IQ measures; a court may consider the full set of IQ data to determine whether subaverage intellectual functioning is actually shown. Non-IQ evidence (including adaptive functioning) has an important role once the intellectual-functioning prong is genuinely in dispute, but Hall/Moore do not constitutionalize a rule that courts must always proceed to adaptive-functioning analysis whenever any score could be adjusted down to 70. Respecting separation of powers and Atkins’ federalism design, Alabama may employ a holistic, cumulative assessment of multiple scores to decide whether the defendant has carried his burden on prong one, so long as it avoids a categorical cutoff rejected in Hall.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Atkins left implementation largely to the States, but Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas require that state frameworks not employ rigid or categorical rules that create an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person, including treating an IQ score as a fixed number rather than accounting for the standard error of measurement. Hall specifically indicates that when IQ evidence is not conclusive, “defendants must be able to present additional evidence” bearing on intellectual disability, which undercuts Alabama’s attempt to end the inquiry based on a pattern of scores in the low 70s without considering validity, interpretation, and other relevant evidence. A holistic evaluation of multiple scores is permissible and often sensible as a factfinding matter, but the Eighth Amendment forbids using multiple above-70 scores as a de facto categorical bar to further consideration where SEM and other evidence could place the defendant within the protected range. Given Hall/Moore’s emphasis on clinical standards, workability, and avoiding bright-line rules, I would affirm that courts may consider multiple IQ scores cumulatively only in a way that still allows consideration of non-IQ evidence when the IQ record is imprecise.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment rule of Atkins, as elaborated in Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas, rejects rigid or de facto IQ cutoffs and requires that IQ testing be treated as imprecise by accounting for the standard error of measurement; when at least one properly administered score (considered with its SEM) reaches or overlaps 70, the defendant must have a fair opportunity to present additional evidence rather than being barred by a tally of other above-70 scores. Hall specifically held that where an IQ score is within the margin of error, the defendant must be allowed to offer “additional evidence” of intellectual disability, and Moore required courts, once the SEM-adjusted range reaches 70, to “move on” to consider adaptive functioning. Alabama’s “likelihood” gloss risks reinstating a numeric cutoff at the intellectual-functioning prong by letting multiple scores in the 70s categorically foreclose consideration of other evidence about the meaning, validity, and clinical interpretation of the scores. Because the Constitution as construed in Hall and Moore permits (and in practice requires) a holistic assessment of multiple IQ scores informed by expert interpretation and relevant non-IQ evidence, the courts below did not err in allowing Smith’s claim to proceed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas require courts to avoid rigid IQ cutoffs and to assess intellectual disability in a manner informed by prevailing clinical standards, including the standard error of measurement, rather than using numerical thresholds as a gatekeeping device that prevents consideration of the broader record. While a State may consider multiple IQ scores, it cannot treat a pattern of above-70 scores as a categorical bar that ends the Atkins inquiry when valid scores (properly interpreted with SEM) leave a meaningful possibility that the defendant’s true IQ is at or below 70, especially where other evidence bears on intellectual functioning and adaptive deficits. Given the procedural posture, Alabama’s effort to recast the governing standard as requiring a showing of “likelihood” (as opposed to a clinically grounded, evidence-based assessment) risks substituting a litigation-friendly rule for the fair, holistic evaluation Hall and Moore contemplate, and it would improperly elevate numerical formalism over the Eighth Amendment’s substantive protection. The Eighth Amendment, as implemented through Atkins and reinforced by Hall/Moore, therefore does not permit foreclosing consideration of non-IQ evidence merely because multiple scores exceed 70, and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)’s parallel bar suggests a narrower approach.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Eighth Amendment permits Alabama courts, in evaluating an Atkins intellectual-disability claim, to treat multiple IQ scores cumulatively to determine whether the defendant has shown significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (including whether a mere theoretical possibility of a true IQ ≤ 70 suffices, or whether a likelihood showing is required).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as applied through Atkins v. Virginia’s categorical bar on executing intellectually disabled persons); relatedly, the general Atkins/Hall/Moore constitutional framework governing state procedures for determining intellectual disability in capital cases (and, by federal interest, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) of the Federal Death Penalty Act).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama (supported by the United States and several amici) argues that the Eleventh Circuit misapplied this Court’s Atkins-line precedents by allowing Smith’s claim to proceed based on a methodology that effectively treats IQ as satisfied whenever multiple scores create a theoretical possibility that his true IQ could be 70 or below. Petitioner contends Alabama may require a threshold showing of likelihood (not mere possibility) that intellectual-functioning prong is met, and may consider the pattern of multiple test results cumulatively—here, five scores (75, 74, 72, 78, 74) that consistently exceed 70—to conclude Smith has not carried his initial burden and thus need not proceed to adaptive-functioning evidence. Petitioner also frames the issue as one of state flexibility and experimentation in evidentiary standards, cautioning against rigid federal superintendence that would unduly restrict state capital sentencing regimes.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith (supported by disability-rights amici) argues that Alabama’s approach, as applied/understood below, violates the Eighth Amendment by using IQ evidence in a way that creates an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person. Respondent contends IQ scores must be interpreted consistent with clinical standards and this Court’s cases, including accounting for measurement error and avoiding bright-line or outcome-driven rules that treat scores above 70 as dispositive. He maintains courts must evaluate intellectual functioning holistically, and once IQ evidence is close enough to the diagnostic range, courts must consider the full body of relevant evidence—including adaptive functioning—rather than using multiple above-70 scores to categorically foreclose further inquiry. Respondent also resists petitioner’s characterization that the lower courts used a mere “possibility” standard, arguing instead they correctly applied constitutional requirements to ensure meaningful consideration of intellectual disability claims.
key_precedents: Clark v. Sweeney (summary reversal referenced in oral argument excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan correctly emphasize Hall and Moore’s functional concern with an “unacceptable risk” that a State’s prong-one screen can become a de facto cutoff that nullifies SEM, but their proposed cure effectively constitutionalizes a near-automatic trigger whenever SEM-adjusted ranges touch 70—something Hall did not hold and Atkins cautioned against by leaving implementation largely to the States. Justice Kavanaugh is right that the Eleventh Circuit’s “mere possibility” formulation invites federal superintendence of state evidentiary thresholds; we can instead reverse narrowly while reaffirming that above-70 scores cannot be treated as dispositive and that any aggregation of multiple scores must genuinely account for measurement error and not operate as a categorical bar. Moore’s alignment-with-clinical-frameworks principle strengthens the as-applied warning against outcome-driven gatekeeping, but it does not compel turning SEM overlap into a per se constitutional rule. On an institutional-legitimacy and precedent-respecting approach, the better course is a limited reversal with clear guardrails against functional cutoffs rather than adopting Respondent’s broader trigger.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s “unacceptable risk” framing is powerful as a policy matter, but it still depends on converting Hall and Moore into a constitutional command that any SEM-adjusted overlap with 70 automatically opens prong two—something neither the Eighth Amendment’s text nor those precedents’ holdings supply. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch note, Hall condemned Florida’s rigid rule that treated an above-70 score as dispositive by ignoring SEM; it did not forbid States from considering the full pattern of multiple scores with SEM in view or from requiring a threshold showing (e.g., likelihood/preponderance) that the defendant is at or below 70 before proceeding. The de facto-cutoff concern Justice Kagan raises is better handled as an as-applied inquiry into whether Alabama’s method functioned as a categorical bar, not by adopting the Eleventh Circuit’s “mere possibility” standard that effectively federalizes state screening rules contrary to Atkins’s delegation. Because respondents’ proposed trigger is untethered to original public meaning and extends our precedents beyond their rationale, my vote remains to reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “unacceptable risk” argument is the most serious objection, and I agree with the Chief Justice that Hall and Moore forbid any approach that functionally makes SEM irrelevant by treating above-70 scores as dispositive. But Sotomayor’s proposed constitutional trigger—whenever an SEM-adjusted range can touch 70, the court must proceed to adaptive functioning—extends Hall’s anti-cutoff principle into a mandatory evidentiary sequence that Atkins did not impose and that our Eighth Amendment precedents do not clearly command. As Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh note, a State may consider the full pattern of multiple scores and require a workable prong-one burden so long as it genuinely accounts for measurement error and does not operate as a categorical bar; the Eleventh Circuit’s “mere possibility” rule looks like generalized federal superintendence rather than correction of a rigid cutoff. Justice Kagan’s de facto-cutoff concern is better addressed through the limiting principle Roberts describes—no nullification of SEM and no automatic dispositiveness—not by constitutionalizing an SEM-overlap gateway for all cases.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point—that Atkins leaves States procedural latitude and Hall did not literally mandate an “any SEM overlap” trigger—does not answer the functional Eighth Amendment question Hall and Moore make dispositive: whether the State’s method, in operation, creates an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person by nullifying measurement error. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, a scheme that aggregates multiple slightly-above-70 scores and then uses a heightened “likelihood” gate to stop at prong one can replicate Florida’s de facto cutoff even if it pays lip service to SEM, because it forecloses the holistic, clinically aligned adaptive-functioning inquiry Moore requires in close cases. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett are right that States may weigh multiple scores and impose a threshold burden, but that discretion ends where the screen operates as outcome-driven gatekeeping that treats acknowledged imprecision as an insurmountable barrier rather than a reason to proceed to prong two. Given the irreversible consequence of execution, I would hold that when SEM-adjusted evidence plausibly places the defendant within the protected range, the Constitution requires access to an adaptive-deficits determination rather than terminating the claim by numerical accumulation alone.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right to worry (as Justice Kavanaugh echoes) that an automatic “any SEM overlap triggers prong two” rule could drift toward federal supervision inconsistent with Atkins’s implementation delegation; Hall does not literally adopt that one-score trigger. But Roberts’s proposed narrowing still understates Hall’s functional holding: the Eighth Amendment is violated when the State’s prong-one screen, in operation, makes SEM irrelevant by treating a cluster of slightly-above-70 scores as effectively dispositive and thereby forecloses any clinically grounded adaptive-deficits inquiry. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s “likelihood” threshold can be permissible only if administered in a way that genuinely incorporates measurement error and does not become outcome-driven gatekeeping—the very “unacceptable risk” Hall and Moore prohibit. On a pragmatic textualist view of those precedents, the workable rule is that when SEM-adjusted IQ evidence plausibly places the defendant in the protected range, the State must permit a holistic determination rather than ending the claim at step one based on aggregated numbers alone.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (joined in substance by Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson) presses the strongest point: that Alabama’s approach can, in operation, create an “unacceptable risk” by making SEM irrelevant and turning slightly-above-70 scores into a functional cutoff. But Hall condemned a rigid, dispositive rule that refused to account for SEM; it did not constitutionalize a mandatory step-two inquiry whenever any SEM-adjusted range could touch 70, and adopting that trigger would, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh warn, convert Atkins’s delegation into federal supervision of state evidentiary gates. The proper constitutional guardrail is narrower: a State may impose a threshold burden and consider multiple scores so long as SEM is actually integrated and no categorical or de facto bar is erected; any abuse is best addressed as an as-applied error rather than by elevating the Eleventh Circuit’s “mere possibility” rule into a general command. On a textualist/originalist understanding of the Eighth Amendment and a faithful reading of our precedents, I do not see Moore extending Hall to require respondents’ one-way ratchet.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “unacceptable risk” argument (joined by Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson) powerfully highlights the Eighth Amendment’s backstop, but it effectively constitutionalizes a trigger—SEM overlap with 70 mandates prong two—that Hall and Moore did not adopt and that sits uneasily with Atkins’s explicit delegation of implementation “to the States.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Hall’s core holding was to forbid treating an above-70 score as dispositive without accounting for SEM; it did not bar States from considering multiple scores in context or from requiring a workable threshold showing so long as SEM is genuinely incorporated and no categorical bar results. I agree with Justice Kagan that de facto cutoffs can arise as applied, but the Eleventh Circuit’s “mere possibility” rule goes beyond preventing Florida-style rigidity and risks turning our precedents into federal supervision of state evidentiary screening. The right course is reversal with a clear limitation: states may not use aggregation or a likelihood gate to nullify SEM and foreclose truly close cases, leaving room for as-applied challenges where that happens.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: a prong-one screen can become a de facto cutoff that creates an “unacceptable risk” under Hall and Moore if it makes SEM functionally irrelevant. But Hall’s holding was narrower—it forbade treating an above-70 score as dispositive by ignoring SEM; it did not constitutionalize a rule that any SEM-adjusted overlap with 70 compels an adaptive-functioning inquiry regardless of the full testing record, and I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh that Atkins leaves States room to impose a workable threshold so long as it is not administered as a categorical bar. The constitutional line, in my view, is not “any plausible SEM overlap triggers prong two,” but whether the State actually accounts for measurement error and avoids outcome-driven rigidity; that concern can be policed through an as-applied inquiry without adopting the Eleventh Circuit’s “mere possibility” standard. Justice Jackson’s fairness concerns reinforce the need for that guardrail, but they do not supply a text- or precedent-grounded limiting principle that would justify the respondents’ near-automatic trigger.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively caution against constitutionalizing an automatic SEM-overlap trigger and against turning Hall into broad federal supervision of state screening rules, and I agree Hall/Moore do not mandate a per se one-score gateway. But that does not resolve the functional Eighth Amendment question Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan highlight: whether Alabama’s aggregation of multiple slightly-above-70 scores plus a heightened “likelihood” gate, as applied, makes SEM effectively irrelevant and thereby recreates the de facto cutoff Hall condemned. Under Moore’s insistence on clinically aligned, non–outcome-driven assessment, when SEM-adjusted ranges plausibly place a defendant within the protected neighborhood, procedural fairness and reliability require access to adaptive-functioning evidence rather than termination at prong one by numerical accumulation. Because execution is irrevocable, I would not reverse on the premise that multi-score weighing and a preponderance threshold are constitutionally adequate without examining whether they operate in practice to foreclose the holistic inquiry Hall and Moore require in close cases.

John Roberts.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left to the States the task of developing workable procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas impose only a limited constitutional constraint: States may not treat a single IQ score as a rigid dispositive cutoff without accounting for the test’s standard error of measurement. Nothing in Hall or Moore clearly forbids a State from considering multiple IQ scores cumulatively—particularly where all administered scores (75, 74, 72, 78, 74) remain above 70—to determine whether the defendant has made the threshold showing of significantly subaverage intellectual functioning, so long as SEM is considered and the approach does not create a categorical bar that forecloses meritorious claims. Given our preference for narrow rulings and respect for state evidentiary standards in this area, I would reverse the Eleventh Circuit to the extent it required Alabama to proceed on a mere theoretical-possibility standard rather than permitting Alabama to require a likelihood showing at the first prong. A limited decision preserving state flexibility while reiterating Hall’s SEM requirement best serves precedent and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment’s text contains no rule prescribing how States must weigh multiple IQ scores or what burden of proof must apply in an Atkins inquiry, and Atkins itself left to the States “the task of developing appropriate ways” to enforce the bar. Hall v. Florida rejected a rigid, dispositive 70-point cutoff that refused to account for the standard error of measurement, but it did not constitutionalize a one-score/one-range rule requiring States to proceed to adaptive-functioning evidence whenever any score’s SEM overlaps 70. Alabama may therefore consider the full set of IQ results cumulatively and require a threshold showing that it is likely—not merely theoretically possible—that the defendant’s true IQ is 70 or below, consistent with federalism and the States’ primary role in criminal procedure. To the extent Moore or Hall is read to compel the contrary, that reading extends those decisions beyond the Constitution’s original public meaning and should be rejected.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left the States substantial latitude to develop procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and neither Atkins nor Hall v. Florida nor Moore requires a rule that any SEM-overlapping or theoretically possible “true IQ” at or below 70 automatically triggers full consideration of adaptive-functioning evidence. Hall forbids a rigid, dispositive 70 cutoff that ignores measurement error, but it does not constitutionalize a mere-possibility standard or bar a State from weighing multiple, consistently above-70 scores cumulatively to decide whether the defendant has carried an initial burden on the intellectual-functioning prong. Permitting Alabama to require a likelihood showing and to consider the pattern of repeated test results is consistent with the Eighth Amendment framework while avoiding a regime that would effectively convert borderline scores into a categorical entitlement and unduly restrict state capital sentencing administration. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach risks turning Hall’s SEM discussion into an inflexible federal supervisory rule, contrary to Atkins’s allocation of responsibility to the States and with serious practical consequences for finality and enforcement of lawful sentences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia and its elaboration in Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas (I & II) require state courts to interpret IQ scores in line with clinical standards, including the standard error of measurement, and to avoid methodologies that create an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person. Under Moore, when the lower end of the SEM-adjusted range for a defendant’s IQ evidence reaches 70 or below, the court must proceed to consider adaptive-functioning evidence rather than using a rigid or outcome-driven gatekeeping rule to end the inquiry at prong one. Alabama’s proposed “cumulative” approach—treating several slightly-above-70 scores as dispositive and demanding a heightened “likelihood” showing before allowing consideration of adaptive deficits—invites precisely the kind of constitutional risk Hall condemned by turning imprecision into a barrier. Given the Eighth Amendment’s categorical bar in Atkins, the Constitution requires procedures that err on the side of fuller consideration where the IQ evidence is close enough to the diagnostic range, especially when the consequence is irreversible.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Atkins bars execution of the intellectually disabled, and Hall and Moore require state procedures that are aligned with accepted clinical practice and do not create an unacceptable risk that a person with intellectual disability will be executed. Hall specifically rejected rigid use of IQ scores—requiring courts to account for the standard error of measurement and not treat a score above 70 as dispositive—so Alabama cannot use a cumulative, multi-score approach in a way that functionally forecloses further inquiry whenever several scores exceed 70 but measurement error leaves a meaningful possibility that true IQ is at or below 70. Moore I/II likewise condemn outcome-driven rules that overemphasize test numbers and underweight the broader evidentiary picture, making it constitutionally problematic to cut off consideration of adaptive-functioning evidence based solely on aggregated IQ results. The Eighth Amendment permits reasonable burdens of proof, but it does not permit a methodology that, in operation, turns SEM into a nullity and blocks holistic assessment where the IQ evidence is close enough to the diagnostic range to require considering the full Atkins framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia bars execution of the intellectually disabled but leaves to the States substantial responsibility for implementing workable procedures, and nothing in the Eighth Amendment’s text or original meaning compels a rule that any theoretical SEM-adjusted possibility of a true IQ ≤ 70 automatically satisfies Atkins’s intellectual-functioning prong. Hall v. Florida rejects rigid cutoffs that treat a single score above 70 as dispositive, yet it also emphasizes that joint analysis of multiple IQ scores is “complicated” and does not constitutionalize a one-low-score (or one-possible-score) rule. Alabama may therefore consider multiple test results cumulatively and require a threshold showing that it is more likely than not—rather than merely possible—that the defendant’s true IQ is 70 or below before proceeding further. To hold otherwise would convert this Court’s Eighth Amendment precedents into a freewheeling federal supervisory regime over state evidentiary standards, in tension with separation-of-powers and federalism principles reflected in Atkins’s allocation of implementation to the States.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia leaves to the States the task of developing workable procedures to enforce the Eighth Amendment’s bar on executing the intellectually disabled, subject to this Court’s guardrails against rigid, outcome-determinative rules. Hall v. Florida and Moore I/II forbid bright-line cutoffs that treat an IQ score just above 70 as dispositive without accounting for measurement error and clinical practice, but they do not constitutionalize a rule that any theoretical possibility of a “true IQ” ≤ 70 compels further proceedings regardless of the full pattern of test results. Alabama may, consistent with Atkins and principles of practical workability and judicial restraint, consider multiple IQ scores cumulatively and require a threshold showing that it is reasonably likely (not merely possible) that the intellectual-functioning prong is satisfied before proceeding to additional evidence, including adaptive-functioning evidence. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach risks converting Hall’s anti-cutoff principle into federal superintendence that displaces state flexibility in evidentiary standards without a clear constitutional command.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Atkins establishes a categorical Eighth Amendment bar on executing the intellectually disabled but leaves to the States the task of implementing workable procedures, subject to the constraint that those procedures not create an unacceptable risk of executing a protected person. Hall v. Florida forbids treating an IQ score above 70 as a categorical cutoff when the score falls within the test’s standard error of measurement, but it does not require a “mere possibility” standard or mandate that any theoretical chance of a true IQ ≤ 70 automatically triggers an adaptive-functioning inquiry. Consistent with Hall and Moore v. Texas, Alabama may evaluate multiple IQ scores cumulatively and may require the claimant—who bears the burden under state law—to show by a preponderance (i.e., likelihood) that he satisfies the significantly-subaverage-intellectual-functioning prong before proceeding further. On this record of five consistently above-70 scores (75, 74, 72, 78, 74), the Eleventh Circuit’s “could be ≤ 70” approach goes beyond what Hall/Moore require and unduly displaces state evidentiary frameworks in an area Atkins expressly left largely to the States.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Atkins v. Virginia and the framework refined in Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas (I & II), state procedures must be “informed by the medical community’s diagnostic framework” and cannot employ rigid or outcome-driven handling of IQ evidence that creates an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person. Alabama’s proposed approach—treating a run of above-70 scores as cumulatively dispositive at prong one and demanding a “likelihood” rather than allowing consideration when scores fall within the standard error of measurement—risks functioning as a de facto cutoff that forecloses meaningful consideration of adaptive deficits despite clinically close scores. Procedurally, the record and oral-argument signals also raise serious fairness concerns about shifting to newly articulated standards and methodologies to justify denying a full Atkins inquiry, particularly where the lower courts understood Hall to require SEM-sensitive interpretation and a holistic assessment once IQ is near the diagnostic range. The Eighth Amendment’s categorical protection in Atkins, as implemented through Hall/Moore, therefore supports requiring Alabama to permit consideration of the full body of relevant evidence rather than ending the analysis based on cumulative above-70 scores alone.
